title: ‘Ferrari comes first’ – Vasseur confirms Hamilton/Leclerc talks
excerpt:
Ferrari Team Principal Fred Vasseur has insisted he is not asking Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc to be “best friends” after holding talks with the pair following their on-track battle at the Mexico City Grand Prix.

The Scuderia drivers went wheel-to-wheel during the opening lap at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez, with the team ultimately missing out on a potential one-two finish after Leclerc received a five-second penalty for the incident involving his team mate Hamilton.

The Briton called for discussions over the rules of engagement between drivers ahead of the Sao Paulo Grand Prix, with Vasseur confirming during Friday’s Team Representatives’ press conference that a meeting had taken place the previous evening.

“We spoke yesterday evening because I had to fly back to Europe between the two races," Vasseur explained.

"It went well. It was good to discuss things and clarify my position and their positions. Now we turn the page and focus on the next one.

"I think they've accumulated a bit of frustration because they're starting each weekend side by side, and you have an accumulation of incidents. At the end of the day, the guidelines are always the same. They need to respect each other. They're two competitors with a fighting spirit, but they need to respect one another.

“Mainly, and firstly, they need to respect the brand, the team, the people working at home and the people working at the track. We're putting a lot of effort into this, and the message was clear and will stay clear."

Vasseur also made clear that Ferrari's interests must remain the priority, acknowledging that the team had collectively fallen short after failing to convert its strong position in Mexico City into victory.

“We failed collectively because we were one-two and didn't win the race in the end," the Ferrari boss added. "The conclusion of the meeting yesterday evening was clear. It was a reminder that Ferrari comes first, for the brand, for the employees and for the Tifosi."

Asked whether managing Hamilton and Leclerc was proving particularly challenging, Vasseur pointed to Ferrari’s recent form and the benefits of having two closely-matched drivers, despite the potential for tensions to rise.

"For sure, we have two experienced, competitive guys," he said.

"It's now four or five races in a row that we've been at the front, scoring the highest number of points after Monza and Madrid. You have an escalation because they both want to win races. I think that's probably the downside of the system. We have two competitive guys starting each weekend next to each other.

"But we are P2 today, because we have two guys who are very close, and we have to manage it. It's a choice in the line-up, and has positives and negatives. But I will deal with the negatives."

Vasseur was also questioned about the relationship between Hamilton and Leclerc, and whether he was concerned by Hamilton’s insistence that he would not be silenced following the events in Mexico.

"I was clear with Lewis, and I'll keep that between Lewis and myself," he responded.

"You can't compare the relationship between Carlos [Sainz] and Charles, Charles and Lewis, or Lewis and Valtteri [Bottas] in the past. They have different personalities.

"I'm not asking them to be best friends. I think that would probably even be a bit negative. I'm just asking them to act and work as professionals, and that's it."

The Frenchman further emphasised the importance of putting Ferrari’s employees first when pressed on whether consequences had been established should similar incidents occur in the future.

"We had a discussion, and it has to stay private. It's a matter of respect for them and for the team," he said.

"We're working for a brand, for sponsors, but mainly for the employees of the team. We've had a good recovery in terms of performance. We came back after Madrid in much better shape, and that's due to the work of the people at home. As a team, we all have to keep this in mind. It's not due to the wind. It's due to the work of the employees of the company."

Mercedes boss Toto Wolff also weighed in on the situation, drawing parallels with the infamous rivalry between Hamilton and Nico Rosberg during their time together at the Silver Arrows.

"It's like déjà vu because you asked me exactly the same questions for so many years, and then Nico called it a day," Wolff said.

"Sometimes, when you put two strong drivers in, the best ones have edges and they want to win. That's a situation that's always very difficult to cope with, particularly under the media spotlight when those cars are racing at the front. I can relate to what Fred is going through at the moment.

"Sometimes it needs a really tough incident to make a point. When I was there with Nico and Lewis, whenever there was an accident, it was understood that this was the limit and it wouldn't continue like that.

"It's about respect for the team – the many thousands of people and the brand they work for. That's what they need to keep in their heads."

title: Komatsu on why fast-tracking Camara was a ‘tough decision’
excerpt:
Haas Team Principal Ayao Komatsu has conceded that promoting Rafael Camara into the squad earlier than expected at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix was a "tough decision", in light of Ryo Hirakawa's solid performance one week earlier in Mexico City.

Camara’s Formula 1 debut at his home race at Interlagos is one of the biggest stories of a busy Sao Paulo GP weekend. The Brazilian had been due to make his first FP1 appearance in a current car with Ferrari, which would have been a useful step towards his planned Haas race debut next season.

However, the sudden departure of Esteban Ocon created an opportunity for the team to fast-track his race debut, accelerating his progress even further.

It might seem the obvious choice to make. However, Komatsu insists that it was not quite that straightforward, especially as Hirakawa did so well when he was called upon in Mexico City, ultimately claiming P10.

The Japanese driver already had a commitment at the Monza World Endurance Championship race for the Interlagos weekend, but it wasn’t necessarily a given that he raced in Italy rather than Brazil.

“It was a tough decision,” Komatsu said on Friday. “Ryo did a fantastic job in Mexico, with such short notice. Yes, he had FP1, but to then jump in the car from FP3 on, to deliver Qualifying, deliver the race, is a huge pressure, huge challenge.

“He's so professional, he's very, very good to work with. And again, his preparation, for somebody to be preparing for that long time, without knowing when that opportunity might arise, it's not easy. You've always got to be ready to perform at your best. But again, full credit to his professionalism. He's been preparing, so when that news was delivered, he was ready, and then he performed.

“So that of course makes my decision difficult here. It was definitely not an easy decision. Maybe from the outside, with who we signed next year, etcetera, it might look like a very easy decision. But it wasn't.”

While giving Camara a head start ahead of 2027 has obvious benefits, there are also potential pitfalls in terms of throwing him in at the deep end with minimal preparation, especially with the added attention that comes with racing in Brazil.

However, when making the call Komatsu was confident that the youngster could cope, especially having seen how he dealt with the Portimao TPC (Testing of Previous Cars) test 'shoot-out' that ultimately won him the 2027 race seat.

Camara looking to learn from Bearman on surprise F1 debut

“There's always pros and cons,” said Komatsu. “It's not a foregone thing that we signed him next year, let's put him as early as possible. There's always a risk.

“Of course, I don't know Rafa for many years, but what I saw in Portimao when we did a shoot-out, how he handled himself, how he contained all that pressure, how he created the environment that let him focus and perform, just everything around it, other than the pure lap time he did, which was impressive. Everything around it for me was very impressive, and such a mature approach.

“So that gave me obviously more confidence that, right, if we go in together [the] message is clear [and] our objective is clear. We can manage.

“If he was somebody who doesn't understand what the professional performing environment should be, if he was somebody that gets really overwhelmed by certain things, or excited by certain things, I would have maybe not have taken this decision. But from everything I saw in Portimao, it was positive, considering this circumstance.”

Komatsu’s views were bolstered by a series of calls with Camara during which those pros and cons were obviously discussed – and the team boss clearly liked what he heard.

“I spoke with Rafa on Sunday night, Monday, Tuesday,” he explained. “All the conversations just reinforced my belief what Rafa can, let's say, not even deliver, but how he can behave or deal with everything, and then shut the noise out. Focus, simplify, and also, not overcomplicate it.

“Again, what I saw in Portimao – conditions were changing all the time, so it was very, very difficult. And then of course, it was huge pressure for him. That was an F1 drive hanging there. But he didn't focus on that result, he didn't focus that I need to produce something to get an F1 drive. He didn't focus on that.

“He really focused on what he's good at, which is the natural, amazing feel he's got, listen to his feel, drive to the conditions. And the conditions honestly lap-by-lap were changing.

“He calmly from the outside did that, managed that mental side, managed that pressure side, not to chase something that is out of your control, just to focus on what you can deliver.

“That was impressive, and if we can take the same mindset here, that's what I believe we can. That's why I made that decision in the end.”

Officially Camara has only been confirmed for Interlagos, with the team yet to confirm their plans for the remaining races of the season.

The obvious catch is that he also has F2 commitments in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, and abandoning the series – and therefore not securing the title – would be a difficult call. Komatsu insists that no decision has been made.

Bearman doesn't see Camara's debut 'as a shoot-out'

“I'd just like to take it one step at a time, really,” he said. “Because again for Rafael, it's a huge challenge. I really want to protect him, and I just don't want to put any external pressure.

“Of course, a complication is he's got the F2 championship as well. In a way I only, let's say, dealt with something I had to deal with, which is this weekend. So that's what we've done.

“And then we really focused on this weekend. It's a huge, huge debut weekend in front of his home crowd. So we really need to manage expectations and clear message, simplify everything, let him focus on what he's brilliant at doing.

“And then that's what we are focusing at this minute. So we just didn't want to get into any other conversation.”

title: Antonelli tops the times from Norris in Sao Paulo FP2
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli ended Friday’s running at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix as the driver to beat, setting the best lap of the day to edge out Lando Norris and Max Verstappen in the second hour of practice.

After a number of teams fielded a rookie driver during FP1, it was back to business as usual with all 22 full-time racers set to take to the track, although the gloomy weather conditions remained in place.

That lack of running for Charles Leclerc, Oscar Piastri, Pierre Gasly, Nico Hulkenberg, Carlos Sainz, and Valtteri Bottas meant that it didn’t take long for the action to get underway when the session began at 1600 local time.

The Alpine man was the first to complete a flying lap on the hard tyres, posting a 1m 14.165s before Leclerc went six-tenths quicker on the grippier medium compound, followed by Antonelli’s 1m 11.857s effort which took the times closer to those set in FP1.

Soon after, Isack Hadjar suggested that it was beginning to drizzle and Leclerc reported feeling an issue with his brakes, with his team mate Lewis Hamilton facing different struggles as he locked up heading into Turn 1.

Elsewhere, there was bad news in the Audi garage – Hulkenberg hadn’t yet ventured onto the circuit, and it was confirmed that he wouldn’t run at all whilst the team worked on the problems that had cut Freddie Slater’s FP1 short.

As the majority joined him in the pits to prepare for the next stage of their respective programmes, Hadjar was left with clear air and made the most of the soft tyres to improve to second place on the timesheets, albeit still behind Antonelli on the hards.

With 35 minutes remaining, George Russell led the pack back out and cut his time down by nearly eight-tenths to surge into P1 with a 1m 11.036s, which rapidly became third once Norris and Verstappen had completed their efforts.

Just 0.020s separated the trio, but Antonelli lowered the benchmark even further and became the first to break into the 1m 10s bracket. As Leclerc tried to edge towards the Italian's lap, he was caught out by Haas’ Rafael Camara on the main straight and was forced to veer towards the wall, losing a chunk of time.

His race engineer confirmed that the incident had added two-tenths to his final lap, worsening Ferrari’s pre-existing deficit to Mercedes that also stood at two-tenths and left him P7.

The focus then switched to long runs, consolidating Antonelli’s hold at the top of the times as he ended the session with a 1m 10.763s. Over two-tenths behind, Norris, Verstappen and Russell maintained their small margins to one another, with Oscar Piastri only slightly further back in the second McLaren.

An unhappy Hamilton was sixth after his tyre-related woes continued, leaving him ahead of Leclerc, home hero Gabriel Bortoleto, Hadjar and Ollie Bearman in the lead Haas.

Franco Colapinto wound up P11 from Racing Bulls’ Arvid Lindblad and Liam Lawson, his Alpine team mate Gasly, Fernando Alonso and newcomer Camara.

Coming to the end of the order, Carlos Sainz took P17 for Willliams to clear Lance Stroll (Aston Martin), Alex Albon (Williams), Cadillac’s Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas, and Hulkenberg, who failed to set a lap time.

title: Camara looking to learn from Bearman on surprise F1 debut
excerpt:
Rafael Camara says he is relishing the opportunity to learn from Ollie Bearman when he makes his unexpected F1 debut for Haas at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix.

Camara has been drafted in following confirmation Esteban Ocon would no longer compete with Haas for the rest of the season, bringing forward the Brazilian youngster’s planned arrival in F1 from 2027.

The 21-year-old was already scheduled to make his FP1 debut for Ferrari at Interlagos, which would have been his first outing in a 2026 car after one TPC session for Haas, and four for the works team.

However, with Camara now thrust into the spotlight at his home event at late notice he believes his fellow Ferrari Driver Academy colleague Ollie Bearman, who he lines up alongside at Haas, can provide a valuable reference.

“I think it would be very good to have Ollie,” said Camara. “He's always been doing a good job. So, [he] will be someone that it will be good to learn [from] and to see what he's doing, so I can also extract for myself and try to put in place.”

He added: "We've been together [at Ferrari] now since the start. Obviously, we were in different categories. He was, I think, going to F3 and I was just starting F4.

"So, obviously, in that way, we were just seeing each other more in the training camps in Ferrari when we were going together, all the drivers.

“So we know [each other] a bit, but not that much. But obviously, from what he showed in F1, what he did, I think it would be a good opportunity to be learning this weekend.”

Camara is also looking forward to experiencing the support of the Brazilian crowd, having felt that backing increasingly as he progressed through the junior categories, and he joins compatriot Gabriel Bortoleto in representing the nation at home this weekend.

“Once I joined F3, where you get more exposure, there was really big support from the Brazilian fans,” he said. “It’s always been nice to see how much they cheer and how much they support you.

“Just being able to do my first Formula 1 race here in front of everyone will be something very special. So for sure, I’ll also try to give them a nice weekend. But like I said, step by step, and just try to do it in a good way.”

title: Norris leads Antonelli and Verstappen in Sao Paulo FP1
excerpt:
Lando Norris finished fastest in Free Practice 1 ahead of the Sao Paulo Grand Prix, the McLaren driver beating Kimi Antonelli and Max Verstappen to top spot.

Norris posted a 1m 11.717s at the Autódromo José Carlos Pace on Friday in Brazil, leaving last year's race winner 0.082s clear of new World Champion Antonelli, with Verstappen just over two tenths back.

Six regular drivers were watching trackside for the opening one-hour session as their cars were driven by rookie drivers, including the likes of Leonardo Fornaroli (in Oscar Piastri's McLaren), Freddie Slater (driving Nico Hulkenberg's Audi) and Colton Herta.

The session was imperative for Herta, with the American driving Sergio Perez's Cadillac and needing to gain one more Super Licence point if the former IndyCar winner is to stand any chance of joining the grid for 2027.

Another rookie to join the field was Rafael Camara, the Brazilian making his Formula 1 debut this weekend in front of his home fans having been promoted early to a race seat at Haas.

Camara, who is joining Haas full-time next season, headed out immediately once the light at the end of the pit lane turned green at 1600 local time, as did a flurry of other drivers for crucial running on a dry track and before any rain materialised.

Drivers soon began exploring the limits, as Lance Stroll, Alex Albon, Lewis Hamilton and Herta all locked up and ran wide at Turn 1 inside the first 10 minutes.

Shortly after a red flag was shown with Slater coming to a stop out on track, this year's F3 runner-up having had his running already curtailed last weekend in Mexico due to reliability problems.

Approaching the 20-minute mark, Antonelli moved to the top of the times with a 1m 12.789s on Pirelli's medium tyre, before lowering the benchmark fractionally to a 1m 12.777s.

Verstappen became the first driver to bolt on a set of softs just before the halfway point, the Dutchman pumping in a 1m 11.953s but stating the downshifts on his car were "unacceptable" over the radio.

Antonelli's first attempt with the soft tyre came to an end at Turn 1 after the Mercedes driver locked up and ran wide, before having another effort which proved more fruitful with a 1m 11.799s.

Team mate George Russell, who will serve a five-place grid penalty for an internal combustion engine change, was three tenths adrift and back in fourth, behind Hamilton's Ferrari.

Norris then moved to the top of the leaderboard, setting a 1m 11.717s just as Albon's session came to an end with 20 minutes remaining, the Williams driver pulling off the circuit with a loss of power steering.

Norris' time remained unbeaten until the chequered flag as drivers and teams focused on long simulations, with the top six completed by Antonelli, Verstappen, who complained his steering was getting harder to turn, Hamilton, Russell and the second Red Bull of Isack Hadjar.

Rookie Gabriele Mini, at the wheel of Pierre Gasly's Alpine, was an impressive seventh ahead of home hero Gabriel Bortoleto (Audi), the second Alpine of Franco Colapinto and Liam Lawson's Racing Bulls.

Fornaroli was P11 from Ollie Bearman's Haas, Aston Martin's Fernando Alonso, Arvid Lindblad (Racing Bulls) and Valtteri Bottas (Cadillac).

Albon finished P16 from Williams team mate Luke Browning (in for Carlos Sainz), Camara, Stroll and Herta.

Dino Beganovic, at the wheel of Charles Leclerc's Ferrari, had his running disrupted by issues which meant the floor of the car was removed for a period of time, while the order was completed by Slater.

title: Russell takes grid penalty at Sao Paulo Grand Prix
excerpt:
George Russell will take a grid penalty at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix due to an engine change, marking his second such penalty in the last four rounds.

Russell was forced to serve a significant penalty at the Singapore Grand Prix due to a range of unavoidable power unit component changes, having retired with a power unit failure one week earlier at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

The Briton had been expected to serve another penalty at some stage during the remainder of the season and that will now happen at Interlagos, with the Mercedes driver discussing the decision to take it at this track in an Instagram Stories post shared by the team.

“I mean, we always had to take a grid penalty at some point between Singapore… obviously we took one in Singapore, but from Singapore until the end of the season,” Russell explained.

“We felt like this was a good place to take it. Lewis [Hamilton] had a big grid penalty here a number of years ago and did pretty well. Five places doesn’t seem that bad, and we’ll try and come back through.”

Hamilton was disqualified from Sprint Qualifying in Brazil back in 2021, forcing him to start the Sprint from the back of the field. He subsequently climbed through the field to fifth before winning Sunday’s Grand Prix from 10th, having taken another penalty.

With the change on Russell’s car being for a fresh Internal Combustion Engine (ICE), the British driver’s penalty has been confirmed as a five-place grid drop.

It comes one week on from a tough weekend in Mexico for Russell, with Team Principal Toto Wolff admitting that the 28-year-old had been “distraught” at the outcome.

title: Bearman doesn’t see Camara’s debut ‘as a shoot-out’
excerpt:
Haas’ Ollie Bearman believes that going up against another Ferrari junior in Rafael Camara doesn’t constitute “a shoot-out”, with the latter set to make his F1 debut on home soil at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix.

Camara had earned a full-time seat with the American squad for 2027, but with Haas’ confirmation that Esteban Ocon will not race for them again this year, the Brazilian’s introduction to the grid was brought forward.

Currently on course to win the F2 title, Camara is yet to drive a 2026 F1 challenger, having only run an old-spec Haas in a test that convinced Team Principal Ayao Komatsu of his raw speed a few months ago.

His first race weekend will therefore be a crucial one in terms of learning, which Bearman is hopeful will give him an idea of how their dynamic as team mates will play out in future seasons.

“I think this is a bit of a preview for next year,” he told the media in Brazil. “I don't see it as a shoot-out but of course it's good to have a team mate that's going to push you – that's what we want as drivers.

“We're competitive, we want to have somebody that's going to force us to level up and I think Rafa will do that, as Esteban did, as all of my team mates have done. I think the eyes are going to be on us but it's an exciting battle.

“For sure it will be a bit more pressure [on Camara] but I think the opportunity of having your first F1 race at home is pretty unique, not many people get that. Only the Australians get that.

“I don't know many people who got to do their first-ever F1 race at home. Of course the circumstances are challenging, but I think it's a great opportunity for him, and I'm really happy for him. To get an F1 debut is one of those key moments in life, so very nice.”

It’s not been the most successful triple header for Bearman, who has failed to finish the last two races and is acutely aware that Audi are now only four points behind Haas in the Teams’ Championship.

However, he also explained that his previous experiences at Interlagos – which included filling in as a last-minute substitute at Haas, similar to Camara’s situation – will help him pursue the best possible result for the team.

Bearman said: “Of course our goal as a team is to try and retain P7 in the Constructors'. Mexico was a challenging weekend for us, losing out on points the way we did, and for the rest of the season we just need to try and score as much as we can, as often as we can.

“This weekend is an opportunity, with the weather as well. It's definitely going to be a challenging one for everybody, especially with Rafa jumping in. But he'll be up to speed quickly I'm sure and let's see how the weather looks.

“Of course I had the opportunity to jump in two years ago where it was a very challenging event, a lot of rain on Sunday especially. But with that weather comes opportunities and I hope that we can make the most of them.

“It's funny how many coincidences there are, but it's nice to be the more experienced driver and I'm excited to see what changes to be honest.

“I feel like I was kind of working towards leading the team and I knew that was a very important role. I don't think much will suddenly change this weekend and the main goal is of course to score points – that doesn't change.”

title: Which rookies are getting FP1 outings in Brazil?
excerpt:
Six F1 teams will field rookie drivers during Friday’s opening practice session for the Sao Paulo Grand Prix, with several familiar faces returning to the track just one week after their outings in Mexico City.

As per the 2026 regulations, every full-time racer must make way for a rookie, defined as someone who has started no more than two Grands Prix, in two practice sessions across the season. The newcomers will have one hour behind the wheel before handing their cars back for FP2, while Rafael Camara is preparing for a different challenge as he makes his full F1 debut for Haas.

But who exactly will be out on track? Here’s an overview of the six drivers taking part in FP1, plus the Brazilian youngster making his first Grand Prix appearance…

Leonardo Fornaroli – McLaren

Leonardo Fornaroli will return to the wheel of McLaren’s MCL40 for the second consecutive weekend after making his third FP1 appearance of the season in Mexico City.

The reigning F2 champion joined McLaren’s Driver Development Programme after securing back-to-back titles in F3 and F2, and has been building his experience through private tests and practice sessions. His preparations included a recent Testing of Previous Cars (TPC) outing at Circuit Paul Ricard, where he completed almost 350 kilometres before finishing P17 in Mexico City’s FP1 session.

After replacing Lando Norris last time out, the 21-year-old will now step into Oscar Piastri’s car at Interlagos, completing McLaren’s mandatory rookie practice allocation.

Dino Beganovic – Ferrari

Ferrari opted not to field a newcomer in the rookie-filled FP1 session in Mexico City, but Dino Beganovic will return to the SF-26 for another appearance with the Scuderia.

A member of the Ferrari Driver Academy since 2020, the 22-year-old Swede has already completed two FP1 outings this year, in Austria and Barcelona. Beganovic impressed during these appearances, finishing eighth in Barcelona and ninth in Austria, where he completed 26 laps.

Currently competing in F2 with DAMS, he will once again replace Charles Leclerc as Ferrari look to gather valuable data during Friday’s opening practice session.

Luke Browning – Williams

Williams Reserve Driver Luke Browning is preparing for his fifth FP1 appearance of the season, following outings in Barcelona, Austria, Italy and Mexico City.

The Briton, who also competes in Japan’s Super Formula championship, was awarded an additional practice opportunity after an electrical issue prevented him from completing any running in Barcelona. Browning returned to the cockpit in Mexico City, completing 33 laps as he continued to familiarise himself with the FW48 and the new regulations.

The 24-year-old will now replace Carlos Sainz at Interlagos, marking his final scheduled rookie outing of the campaign after stepping in for Alex Albon last time out.

Freddie Slater – Audi

Freddie Slater will be hoping for a smoother experience as he returns to Audi’s R26 following a disrupted first F1 practice appearance in Mexico City.

The 18-year-old, who became the first member of Audi’s Driver Development Programme earlier this year, saw his running compromised after a cooling fan was inadvertently left attached to his car, resulting in a €7,500 fine for the team.

After finishing runner-up in F3 this season, the Briton is preparing to step up to F2 with Invicta Racing in 2027.

He will replace Nico Hulkenberg in Brazil after driving Gabriel Bortoleto’s car in Mexico City.

Gabriele Mini – Alpine

Gabriele Mini will make his second consecutive FP1 appearance for Alpine after his official F1 weekend debut in Mexico City.

A member of the Alpine Academy since 2023, the Italian previously completed Testing of Previous Cars (TPC) running in July before stepping into Franco Colapinto’s A526 at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez.

The 21-year-old finished P14, just over seven tenths behind Pierre Gasly, despite a Virtual Safety Car disrupting his final soft-tyre run.

Currently fourth in the F2 standings with two victories and seven further podiums, Mini will return to the cockpit at Interlagos, this time replacing Gasly.

Colton Herta – Cadillac

Colton Herta will make his sixth FP1 appearance of the season as the American continues his pursuit of the Super Licence points required to compete in F1.

The former IndyCar driver has been balancing his F2 campaign with test driver duties for Cadillac, completing practice outings in Barcelona, Hungary, Italy, Austin and Mexico City. Currently 19th in the F2 standings, Herta has impressed Cadillac during his F1 appearances and remains a potential candidate for a future race seat.

After falling short of the required mileage in Mexico City, the 26-year-old needs to complete at least 100 kilometres on Friday to secure his final Super Licence point.

He will replace Sergio Perez in Sao Paulo after stepping into Valtteri Bottas’ car last time out.

Rafael Camara – Haas

While the other rookies will hand their cars back after FP1, Rafael Camara is preparing for his full Formula 1 debut in front of his home crowd.

The 21-year-old Brazilian, who currently leads the F2 standings and has secured titles in Formula Regional and F3, was originally due to join Haas as a full-time driver in 2027.

However, his debut has been brought forward following the team confirmed Esteban Ocon would no longer compete for them, with reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa replacing the Frenchman in Mexico City and scoring a point on his F1 debut.

Hirakawa’s World Endurance Championship commitments have since opened the door for Camara, who impressed Haas during a TPC outing at Portimao in August.

A member of the Ferrari Driver Academy since 2021, Camara will partner Ollie Bearman for the entire weekend. He has never raced at Interlagos or driven the team’s 2026 challenger, but will have three practice sessions to get up to speed ahead of Qualifying.

Haas have yet to confirm who will occupy the seat for the remaining rounds of the season.

title: F1 rookie learns stewards fate after 'clearly dangerous' Charles Leclerc incident
excerpt:
F1 rookie Rafael Camara has escaped with a reprimand despite ignoring "multiple" radio warnings that led to a "clearly dangerous" incident involving Charles Leclerc.

Midway through FP2 at Interlagos, Camara, handed his F1 debut this weekend with Haas, was dawdling on the racing line, climbing the hill in the final sector as Leclerc's Ferrari came through on a flying lap.

Leclerc was squeezed towards the outside wall at high speed, but escaped without damage - although he did make his displeasure at Camara known, with the incident reported to the stewards for an investigation.

After speaking with Camara, team representatives, and reviewing video, team radio and in-car video evidence, the stewards found that "car 51 was warned multiple times that car 16 was arriving on a fast lap.

"Yet, car 51 was weaving and moving well into the racing line. Car 16 had to take evasive action to avoid a collision by moving to the right, with a significant amount of the car off the track.

"The situation that was created was clearly dangerous and car 51 should have taken more care to avoid impeding car 16.

"While the typical penalty for impeding in a Free Practice session is a warning, in this instance, we are of the view that a reprimand is warranted."

title: Kimi Antonelli names major challenge facing every F1 driver at Sao Paulo GP
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has described how the bumps under braking at Turn 1 at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix will be a challenge all weekend.

The world champion finished second and first in the two Friday practice sessions, but the two outings were blighted by drivers running wide after locking up for the first downhill left of the Senna S.

The bumps under braking, coupled with low tyre temperatures, combined to make braking tricky, with laps being instantly ruined if drivers were required to cut across the run-off - which Antonelli did on his first soft tyre lap in FP1.

Reflecting on the situation, the Mercedes driver explained how he was trying to modulate the brake pressure to find the right balance.

"It's quite bumpy [into Turn 1], so it is not easy to find the right braking spot because the grip is coming up and you try to brake later and later," Antonelli said.

"It is quite bumpy, so it is hard to manage brake pressure, so it is not easy, and I was trying to do a little bit more, but it was a bit too much."

Turning to his day overall, Antonelli felt there were still improvements to be made to his W17 on the longer runs.

"I felt good with the car over a single lap, but on the long run, there's a bit of work to do, but overall, I am feeling good and excited for [qualifying].

"I think we have a good chance for [qualifying], however, we're all very close.

"McLaren is strong as well. Red Bull is strong, so we just try our best to be ready. Also, we'll see how the weather is going to be, but I'm really excited.

"The track is a lot of fun. The grip is a bit low, but I'm trying to do my best."

title: Liam Lawson backed for new F1 option if Racing Bulls swing axe
excerpt:
Former F1 driver Martin Brundle has backed Liam Lawson to find a seat on the grid elsewhere if he is dropped by Racing Bulls.

The New Zealander has not yet heard whether he will be retained by the Faenza-based squad for next year despite his impressive run of performances.

Lawson has consistently placed himself in the point-scoring positions this year and sits ninth in the drivers' championship, the leading performer outside of the drivers at the top four teams.

The 24-year-old is facing competition for his seat from F2 title protagonist Nikola Tsolov, who made his FP1 debut with the team in Mexico.

Brundle insisted F1 is a “brutal business” as the wait for Lawson goes on.

“That's very strange, isn't it?” Brundle said, speaking to Sky F1.

“He's done such a great job, he's scored so many points. They're comfortably fifth in the world championship.

“But this is a brutal business, and you get a chance to drive an F1 car because somebody else has been kicked out.”

Regardless of what decision is made regarding Lawson, Brundle is adamant it will not spell the end of his F1 career.

“Watching Esteban [Ocon]'s name come down [in Mexico], it did seem like the front of a bus or the front of a train changing names quite frequently. It's very unusual these days.

“But Liam has done enough to stay in F1. If he's not got that job, he'll either be a super sub, or he'll get a slot quite quickly somewhere else.

“He's been outstanding this year, but it depends on what the team wants to project for the future.”

title: F1 champions trade places as mist descends on Sao Paulo GP practice
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli underlined his new-found status as F1 champion by comfortably setting the fastest lap in a Friday practice for the São Paulo Grand Prix that was blighted by mist.

Free of the burden of bidding for the title, and after recovering from an illness that affected him during last weekend's Mexico City GP in which finishing third was enough to see him crowned as F1's youngest champion, Antonelli was the only driver who managed to dip into the 1:10s for a lap around the renowned Interlagos.

Under a cloud bank that slowly descended over the circuit as the session wore on, and with low track temperatures ahead of a weekend set to be heavily affected by rain, Antonelli posted a time of one minute 10.763s on the soft-compound Pirellis.

It easily pushed McLaren's Lando Norris off top spot by a quarter of a second, and reversed the standings at the end of FP1 when the Briton finished fastest by 0.082s ahead of the 20-year-old.

Max Verstappen, as was the case in FP1, was third quickest in his Red Bull, with the four-time F1 champion, Norris and George Russell in his Mercedes in fourth, separated by just 0.020s.

[Article continues below]

On his first push lap in the opening few minutes of the session, Antonelli posted the third-quickest lap of the day, only bettered by his own and that of the leading time from Norris in FP1, with a 1:11.857s on hard tyres.

The Italian came within three thousandths of a second of that lap on his next outing before the long runs unfolded. At that stage, Norris was second fastest, 0.209s adrift, followed by Verstappen, a further 0.075s down, both on the medium compound.

A trait from FP1 that continued throughout FP2 was the number of drivers needing to use the sizeable run-off area out of Turn 1, heading into the Senna S.

The issue appeared to be a bump on the approach into the downhill left-hander, forcing drivers - including the likes of Antonelli and Russell - off track.

Twenty-five minutes into the session, Russell was the first driver to venture out on the soft tyres, and he immediately went quickest with a time almost eight-tenths faster than Antonelli.

It was a benchmark rapidly wiped out by Norris by 0.020s before Verstappen split the pair, finishing six-thousandths adrift of the outgoing champion.

Antonelli, though, showed his hand soon after, setting the lap that remained unbeaten through to the end of the session.

McLaren's Oscar Piastri was fifth quickest, 0.321s adrift, with the Ferraris of Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc surprisingly off the pace in sixth and seventh at a track many believed would suit the SF-26s.

Hamilton was 0.450s down and Leclerc, who missed FP1 as reserve Dino Begovic took up the Monégasque's seat, finished 0.720s adrift.

Audi's Gabriel Bortoleto, Isack Hadjar in his Red Bull and Haas' Oliver Bearman completed the top 10, the latter 1.228s behind Antonelli.

Cadillac's Valtteri Bottas was the slowest of those who set a time in 21st, finishing 2.620s adrift.

Sadly for Audi's Nico Hulkenberg, he failed to even get into the car due to a terminal issue initially encountered by reserve Freddie Slater in FP1 that restricted the 18-year-old to seven laps.

The stewards only have one investigation to mull over, that involving Haas rookie Rafael Camara, the Brazilian making his F1 debut in front of his home crowd this weekend, but caught heavily impeding Leclerc.

title: Nico Hulkenberg suffers Brazil disaster after early rookie Audi failure
excerpt:
Nico Hulkenberg will not drive on track at all on Friday at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix after technical gremlins on his Audi car.

Hulkenberg had stood down for FP1 at Interlagos in favour of Freddie Slater, but for the second straight weekend, the young Briton suffered a stoppage on track early in FP1.

The car was recovered back to the garage, where the team worked to diagnose the issues, but whilst the issue was identified, it was not able to be fixed in time.

Audi communicated that the German was formally out of the second practice session 17 minutes into the running.

Hulkenberg's car was seen to be up on the jacks with mechanics working underneath the machine around the time he was formally ruled out of the session.

title: Toto Wolff offers first insight into Esteban Ocon axe from Haas
excerpt:
Toto Wolff has offered a glimpse into the difference of opinion that led to Esteban Ocon's axe by Haas over last weekend's Mexico City Grand Prix.

Haas confirmed on Saturday morning that Ocon would not drive for the team for the remainder of the weekend.

The decision followed a heated radio exchange during second practice in Mexico, when Ocon contested a call from engineer Laura Mueller to switch his high-fuel run from soft to medium tyres. It is understood the situation escalated in the Friday debrief with team principal Ayao Komatsu, who has refused to go into detail on what was said.

Ryo Hirakawa deputised for Ocon across the remainder of the weekend at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez. After post-race penalties were handed out, the Japanese collected a point for a 10th-place finish.

On Tuesday, Haas announced Ocon would not drive for the team in the remaining four grands prix of the season, bringing his time with Haas to an abrupt end.

For this weekend, Rafael Camara, previously announced as Ocon's replacement for next season, will make his F1 debut in front of his home crowd in the São Paulo Grand Prix.

Wolff, who has known Ocon since his junior career, is the first senior paddock figure to speak publicly about the breakdown, framing it as a clash between Komatsu's need to protect his team and Ocon's conviction that he had done nothing wrong.

Speaking about the situation to the media, including RacingNews365, Mercedes team principal Wolff said Komatsu had been left with no choice but to act.

"At the end it came to the point where Ayao needed to represent the team and protect the team from certain rhetoric," said Wolff.

"On the other side, Esteban felt that personally, he wasn't wrong in the things he said.

"You've got to respect that in the end the team calls the shots. The team principal needs to decide when it's enough, and that is what Ayao did."

[Article continues below]

Wolff details remarkable Vasseur deal for Ocon big break

Wolff's comments carry weight given his long history with Ocon, stretching back to the Frenchman's junior single-seater days. The Austrian explained how Mercedes first took on managing Ocon's career through driver development advisor Gwen Lagrue, before helping fund his route into Formula 1.

"So at Mercedes, we picked up the management of Esteban, due to Gwen," said Wolff. "That's how we got to know Gwen, when Gravity defaulted, and then we agreed to work with Fred [Vasseur] in GP3. We won the championship together.

"Then there wasn't really an opportunity in Formula One. Then the DTM door opened, and we did that together."

Then detailing a remarkable situation between Mercedes and Vasseur that helped give Ocon his F1 break, Wolff said: "I don't know if this is known, when suddenly there appeared to be a free seat at Manor from Spa onwards [2016 Belgian GP], it needed $2 million.

"We said we could provide $1 million for that seat, but we were missing $1 million, and Fred put the money in personally to give Esteban the opportunity.

"Over all those years, I think we were all very supportive and very strong in trying to make sure that Esteban would have the best possible opportunity."

title: Ferrari reveal outcome of crunch Hamilton-Leclerc meeting after Mexico spat
excerpt:
Ferrari has held a meeting with Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc following their spat in Mexico City which cost the team a one-two.

Ferrari boss Fred Vasseur has explained how drivers Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc are now fully aware of their "guidelines" after a crunch meeting in Brazil.

The row between the drivers was sparked by Leclerc's action on the opening lap of the Mexico City Grand Prix, where he attacked around the outside of Hamilton at Turn 4.

Both cars went off the track, with Hamilton delayed just enough to allow Max Verstappen to sneak up the inside to grab second place - behind Leclerc, who was then handed a five-second time penalty by the stewards.

Ultimately, Hamilton felt this action had cost the team a one-two finish, as he said over the radio that the team had "big problems", and then declared post-race he was "really pi**ed" at Leclerc and the situation, whom he said had a "do or die" attitude on-track.

Vasseur then accused both drivers of showing a "lack of respect" to Ferrari in the incident, with the trio holding a crunch meeting on Thursday of the Sao Paulo Grand Prix weekend.

"It went well. It was good to discuss, good to clarify my position and their position," Vasseur told media, including RacingNews365, about the meeting.

"It was good to do, and now we turn the page, and we are focused on the next race.

"The guidelines are still the same. I think they have accumulated perhaps a bit of frustration because they are starting each weekend side-by-side and you have an accumulation effect.

"But at the end of the day, the guidelines are always the same: they need to respect each other. They are two competitors with the fighting spirit for sure, but they need to have respect for the other one.

"But mainly and firstly, they need to respect the brand, the team, the people working at home, the people working on track. I think we are putting in a lot of effort on this, and the message was clear, and will stay clear."

[Article continues below]

© XPB Images

Ferrari hold crunch Hamilton-Leclerc talks

When then asked if dealing with the Hamilton-Leclerc dynamic was the most challenging of his career, Vasseur explained that he was prepared to deal with the negatives.

"We have two experienced guys, two competitive guys, and it is now four or five races in a row that we are scoring the highest number of points after Monza and Madrid," he said.

"For sure you have that kind of escalation that you all want to win races, and I think it's probably the downside of the system is that we have two competitive guys starting each weekend next to each other, but I think if we are P2 today [in the constructors'], it's also because we have two guys who are very, very close, and we have to manage it.

"But it's a choice; it's a choice of the lineup. And I have the positive and the negative, but I will deal with the negative."

Vasseur was then pushed on whether the two drivers had agreed to work together for the sake of the team, where he indicated that Ferrari "had failed."

"It is true for every single team that on the grid the drivers are working for the team and the team has to come first," he said.

"For sure, in this situation, we failed collectively because we were one-two, and we didn't win the race in the end.

"That means that it's clear that we failed, and we have to react. But the conclusion of the meeting yesterday evening was clear.

"It was a clear reminder that Ferrari is coming first. It's coming first for the brand, for the employees, for the Tifosi, and we have to keep this in mind."

title: Valtteri Bottas insists Cadillac seat safe despite growing F1 axe rumours
excerpt:
Valtteri Bottas has insisted he remains relaxed about his Cadillac future, despite mounting speculation that Colton Herta could replace him for 2027.

The Finn, who joined Cadillac for its debut season alongside Sergio Perez, holds a multi-year deal to extend his stay into 2027. That option has yet to be formally triggered by the American outfit, fuelling talk in the paddock that a change could be coming.

Herta, who has been building super licence points through a string of Free Practice 1 outings this season, has emerged as a leading contender for the seat, with Cadillac having made no secret of its ambition to field an American driver.

Following his latest first practice appearance in São Paulo, the American driver does now have the necessary points total to race in F1.

Speaking to select media, including RacingNews365, Bottas admitted he had been taken aback by the scale of the rumours.

"I'm quite surprised about the amount of noise on that because I know what my situation is, and yeah, all I've heard is that the team has been happy with what I'm doing," Bottas said.

"But at the same time, we know how this sport works, and especially now, everyone wants to be in Formula 1, and if somebody sees an opportunity somewhere, they're going to try and go for it, one way or the other.

"But yeah, the way our team is structured and the way decisions are made for the future, everything needs to be approved by the board. And I believe that meeting is still yet to happen. But yeah, I've been convinced that nothing has changed. So that's where we are."

Valtteri Bottas agrees Cadillac axe would be a surprise

Herta is not the only external name being linked to Bottas' cockpit. Mercedes reserve driver Fred Vesti has also been positioning himself as a candidate, having impressed in Mexico by finishing third in Free Practice 1 while standing in for George Russell, just 0.111 seconds behind Kimi Antonelli.

The Dane's ties to General Motors, having raced and won titles for Cadillac in IMSA sports car competition, have only strengthened the chatter.

Asked how odd it would be if Cadillac were to question his performances after a season of following team instructions and utilising his experience, Bottas replied: "I agree. Yeah, it would be very odd. So that's why I don't think anything is going to change with my situation.

"That was kind of always the deal, and all season I've been really following instructions, and sometimes it has been very clear that I should just try and get the car over the finish line.

"But of course, there are always people who look from the outside. They don't maybe understand the big picture, and then you get the criticism, which is normal in the sport.

"But it's just the main thing is that we know where we are. I know that, I know what my job is, and if they want something further from me, then I'm sure they will tell me."

title: Dan Ticktum fronts Fortescue Formula E launch amid Taylor Barnard legal battle
excerpt:
Fortescue Zero Racing officially launched on Thursday, revealing its livery at Shoreditch Electric Light Station in London ahead of its maiden Formula E campaign.

The British-based, Australian-licensed outfit was formed through Fortescue's acquisition of Penske Autosport and will compete under Gen4 regulations from the 2026/27 season, running Jaguar customer powertrains out of its Kidlington base.

Dr Andrew Forrest, Fortescue's founder and executive chairman, attended the launch alongside company CEO and former Argentina rugby captain Gus Pichot.

Also present were Claire Williams, who serves as a global brand ambassador for Fortescue Zero without holding an operational role at the team, and team principal Jim Wright, whose background spans senior roles at Williams, Toro Rosso and Virgin Racing in Formula 1 before a decade embedded in Formula E leadership with Mahindra, Venturi and Andretti.

"We’re not here to blend in. We’re here to build a team that competes, does things differently and

earns its place on the grid," said Wright.

"This is the world’s first look at who we are. But the real work is well underway, to be ready, push

hard and deliver as a team when we begin running on-circuit next week.

"Launching a new racing outfit is a significant challenge, and that’s exactly what makes it exciting.

We have strong foundations, an experienced, talented and highly motivated group and we’re

ready to compete."

Dan Ticktum, confirmed as one half of the team's debut driver line-up, was also in attendance. The Briton joins from Cupra Kiro, where his exit followed internal friction over disciplinary and contractual matters.

RacingNews365 attended Fortescue Zero's first Formula E launch, with it unveiling an exciting black and green livery for the upcoming campaign. The livery contains hidden details of Fortescue's birth, what it believes in and where it is heading, including nods to Dr Forrest and Sir Frank Williams.

Crucially, the team's other driver, Taylor Barnard, was not in attendance.

Taylor Barnard absence a notable launch factor

Taylor Barnard, the other driver signed to partner Ticktum, was notably absent from proceedings.

According to Formula E Notebook, His management company, PHM Racing Academy, has lodged a legal challenge seeking to void his Fortescue Zero contract, aiming to free the driver to explore other options for the Gen4 debut season.

Fortescue Zero maintains that Barnard remains contractually bound to the team, but the dispute meant the driver skipped the launch entirely.

It remains unclear whether the legal challenge will succeed or whether Barnard will ultimately line up for the team when testing gets underway in just over a week.

title: Lewis Hamilton spying 'number one spot' opportunity inside Ferrari - Brundle
excerpt:
Martin Brundle believes Lewis Hamilton is using the fallout from last weekend's Mexico City Grand Prix clash with Charles Leclerc to strengthen his position inside Ferrari.

Hamilton finished second in Mexico after Leclerc attempted a move around the outside of Turn 4, running wide and cutting across the grass before retaking the lead. The stewards handed Leclerc a five-second penalty rather than the standard ten, judging that both cars carried excessive speed into the corner. The sanction did not restore the lead to Hamilton, however. Max Verstappen inherited the win, with Hamilton classified second, 0.799s back, and Leclerc dropping to fourth.

Hamilton made his frustration clear over team radio during the race, and Brundle, speaking as a pundit, said the seven-time champion is now unfiltered about Ferrari's internal dynamics.

"He's at the stage of his career, life, where he's going to be unfiltered, and he was pretty unhappy with what happened," Brundle said.

"He said on the radio that they've given Charles the win today with just that five-second penalty, and it's definitely worth cutting a few corners, getting out front, you make a lot more than five seconds.

"But the big story is, it didn't give a Ferrari driver the win at all, it gave Max Verstappen the victory, as it happened.

"So it wasn't the smartest move in Charles's career and life, trying to go around the outside of Turn 4 there. That was a 75-25 move against your teammate. It just wasn't a smart move.

"Lewis is upset. He's realised there's a chance to actually make a bit of ground on this because that was a bit silly.

"But you know, I was thinking about this in the week. When I first was in Formula 1, I think we had 40 people in the team. Now there are 2000 people in the team.

"You've got the situation where they say you're representing 2,000 people, and it's true, but you're in Formula 1 as an individual sports person. You're measured as an individual sports person in a team environment, and now that team's 2,000 people, it's almost becoming impossible."

Drawing on what has unfolded inside McLaren in recent seasons, Brundle added: "I think we saw the same with Lando and Oscar.

"Where do you stand as a driver? I think this is a new challenge of, where do I really stand here? You can't just keep criticising me for racing for myself just because I'm in a team. It actually doesn't work, does it? If you think about it."

[Article continues below]

Brundle - 'I stand by what Lewis said'

Brundle drew a parallel with Hamilton's combustible years alongside Nico Rosberg at Mercedes, where incidents at Monaco and Spa in 2014 forced the team to draw up formal rules of engagement.

"I seem to remember him and Nico running into each other quite dramatically on a few occasions, having quite a spat. It's inevitable," Brundle said.

Before then turning again towards a possible end-game for Hamilton, and comments that will have been picked up by Ferrari chairman John Elkann and CEO Benedetto Vigna.

"I stand by what he said," remarked Brundle. "I think Lewis has realised there's a really good platform to carve himself out more of a number one spot there, more clout in that situation. He's not going to let that go.

"And that comment when he got out of the car during the red flag of 'We've got big problems here! Big problems!' That wasn't to anybody around in Mexico. That was to some people in Italy."

title: Lando Norris tops Brazil FP1 with upgraded McLaren ahead of new champion Kimi Antonelli
excerpt:
Lando Norris has topped the opening practice session at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix weekend, as McLaren's upgraded car enjoyed a strong debut in Brazil.

The Woking-based squad is the only team to bring a substantial upgrade to Interlagos, and it looked rapid in Norris' hands, as he ended the session ahead of Kimi Antonelli.

The outing marked Antonelli's first event since being crowned world champion at the Mexico City Grand Prix a handful of days ago.

Max Verstappen was third for Red Bull, but noted some issues he was having during the 60-minute session, which related ot his gear shifts and steering.

[Article continues below]

Lewis Hamilton was fourth for Ferrari and was one of many drivers who had a rookie team-mate behind the wheel for the session.

Dino Beganonvic stood in for Charles Leclerc, who arrived late in Brazil following the birth of his daughter. Beganovic was only 21st, having been forced to abandon his hot lap due to an issue with his car.

George Russell was fifth in the second Mercedes, ahead of Isack Hadjar.

Gabriele Mini produced a highly respectable effort for Alpine as he ensured he ended the day as the fastest rookie in the session.

He managed to set a lap that was one-tenth faster than full-time driver Franco Colpainto, with one of the local favourites, Gabriel Bortoleto, lodged between the two Alpines.

Liam Lawson, who is still awaiting news about his F1 future, rounded out the top 10.

The FP1 outing was a crucial one for Colton Herta, who managed to clock 30 laps and finally secure enough points to obtain his F1 super licence.

Rafael Camara, who is making his F1 debut this weekend with Haas, ended the day in 18th place.

It was an early end to the session for Audi rookie Freddie Slater, who stood in for Nico Hulkenberg.

Just seven laps into his stint, Slater pulled to the side of the track as he reported an issue with the car, resulting in an early red flag.

He was not the only driver who was forced to pull over, as Alex Albon stopped with just under 20 minutes in the session - however, his car was able to be cleared with a red flag intervention.

title: 2026 F1 Sao Paulo Grand Prix - Brazil Free Practice 1 results
excerpt:
Lando Norris took first practice honours for the São Paulo Grand Prix, with Kimi Antonelli in his slipstream on the timesheet at Interlagos.

McLaren driver Norris set the pace around one of the best circuits on the calendar with a lap of one minute 11.717s. Antonelli, who will replace Norris as F1 champion next season, finished just 0.082s behind in his Mercedes.

Red Bull's Max Verstappen was just under a quarter of a second adrift in third, with Lewis Hamilton in his Ferrari a tenth further back.

title: Now it's official! Colton Herta finally has his FIA superlicence
excerpt:
After a bizarre mistake a week ago in Mexico City, Colton Herta has now officially qualified for an FIA superlicence, paving the way for a potential move to an F1 race seat in 2027.

Herta took over Sergio Perez's Cadillac during first practice for the São Paulo Grand Prix and, after completing the 24 laps needed at Interlagos, chalked up the 100km of running required to earn a point towards his superlicence.

On Friday in Mexico City, the first free practice hour at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez was supposed to help the American reach the required 40-point threshold needed to race in F1.

This is because rookie stand-in drivers for those sessions earn a solitary superlicence point if they complete 100km. Herta therefore needed to complete 24 laps, and racked up 30.

However, it was established soon after the session that a mistake on the IndyCar website incorrectly listed him as finishing sixth in the standings last year, when, in actuality, he finished seventh.

Therefore, he earned two fewer superlicence points than the six that were originally thought. The FIA confirmed later that Herta remained on 39.

It highlighted that Cadillac's maths was wrong when approached by RacingNews365 ahead of the race in Mexico, with the team insisting he was on 39 points and one away.

In reality, the nine-time IndyCar winner secured one point in 2023, 30 in 2024 when he finished second in the American championship, and four last year.

Those 35 points, coupled with the four he has earned for first free practice sessions for Cadillac this year — in Barcelona, Austria, the United States, and then Mexico — brought the F2 driver to 39 of the 40 required.

Allowed to run in FP1 at Interlagos, Herta completed the 24 laps needed with seven minutes of the session remaining.

title: British rookie sparks São Paulo practice red flag as Audi misery strikes again
excerpt:
Freddie Slater suffered practice misery for the second successive Friday after the Audi youngster ground to a halt just 15 minutes into the opening session ahead of the São Paulo Grand Prix.

A week ago, in the build-up to the race in Mexico City, the team's rising star, who finished second on his debut in F3 this season and will move up to F2 next year with the front-running Invicta team, endured a miserable outing.

The 18-year-old, who was the first driver to be brought into Audi's driver development programme following the team's entry into F1 this season, was sent out on track at one stage with a cooling fan still inside the right-hand sidepod of his car.

Slater was naturally recalled to the pits by Audi to have the fan removed, leading the stewards to investigate the team after the session for his car being released in an unsafe condition.

It left Slater with just six laps to his name at that stage, and without a time on the board at the bottom of the timing sheet.

Slater, who had taken over Gabriel Bortoleto's car for the session, did finally return to the track with 11 minutes remaining, going on to eventually post a time that lifted him off the bottom of the standings.

A week at Interlagos, Slater, in for Nico Hulkenberg on this occasion, had completed just seven laps, with a best of one minute 14.966s on the hard tyres, when his car stopped on track, sparking a red flag.

Audi described it as "an issue" it would "investigate the problem fully as soon as the car is back in the garage".

title: Damon Hill offers Ferrari simple Hamilton-Leclerc solution: 'Ends all debate'
excerpt:
Damon Hill believes Ferrari has a straightforward way out of its Lewis Hamilton-Charles Leclerc mess: make the seven-time F1 champion the team's clear number one driver.

The debate around the Scuderia flared up again after the Mexico City Grand Prix, where Hamilton started from pole position but had to fight hard to keep Charles Leclerc behind him on the opening lap.

It went wrong at Turn 4, where both drivers ran off the track. Leclerc then took the lead by cutting across the circuit, leaving Hamilton to settle for third place behind Max Verstappen.

Leclerc was later handed a five-second penalty for the move, but Verstappen used the pit-stop window to seize the lead himself.

It meant Hamilton missed out on a win that had been within his grasp. He made clear afterwards that he wants rules put in place at Ferrari to stop such clashes happening again, bearing in mind what also happened at Monza and Zandvoort recently.

Hill, the 1996 F1 champion, feels Ferrari can put a stop to it.

Hill, via X, wrote: "Here is where I stand on the Lewis v Charles debate, and I made this point in my commentary on Sunday in Mexico.

"Make Lewis #1 Ferrari driver. Sort it out. Make it clear. Ends all debate. Lewis will deliver for Ferrari. If they back him 100%"
